text: External Editor 是面向 DSH Web 客户端的外部编辑器插件。在会话标题栏加入分栏选择器，列出运行 DSH 的主机上已检测到的编辑器、终端和文件管理器，并可将当前会话目录交给所选应用打开。常用选择会保存在浏览器中，之后可直接点击打开，也能从菜单切换应用。插件通过主机端目录检测和启动应用，并提供应用列表、图标及打开会话目录的路由；支持的应用可按平台探测，也可通过配置替换目录表。适合希望从 DSH 会话快速跳转到项目文件或终端的开发者。应用在 DSH runtime 所在主机启动；不需要额外 API 密钥或外部服务。

External Editor adds a picker to the DSH web session header. It detects editors, terminals, and file managers on the runtime host, then opens the session directory in the selected app. The browser remembers the last choice. No API key or external service is required.
想从 DSH 会话标题栏一键把当前项目目录交给本机编辑器打开。
能不能在 DSH 里挑选已安装的终端或文件管理器来查看会话工作目录？
Open the current DSH workspace in the editor I chose last time.
External Editor 的功能「会话目录快速打开」：在 DSH 会话标题栏选择已检测到的编辑器、终端或文件管理器，将当前会话目录作为工作目录启动所选应用；上次选择会保存在浏览器中，便于下次直接打开。

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · omdsh-editor：English | [中文](README.zh.md)

Open the project you are working in with the editor you actually use. A split control in the [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) web GUI's session header: press the left half and the conversation's directory opens in the editor you chose last time, press the chevron and pick a different one.

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · omdsh-editor：The harness has no such capability and no seam that would let one be reached around it, so this package adds both halves — the host side that finds the applications and starts one, and the browser side that offers them.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────┐
│  my-project                                  │  ⌗   ⧉   [◧|▾] │  ← the session header
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────┘
                                                        │

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · What it adds：| Surface | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| The split editor control, at the right of the session header | One entry in `conversation.session.header.utilities`, the utility row ui-conversation already declares |
| `GET /omdsh-editor/editors` | The applications this host actually has, and its `process.platform` — a `stat` per catalog row, cached for 15 seconds |
| `GET /omdsh-editor/icon?id=…` | Each application's own icon, read out of the copy installed on this host and served as PNG |
| `POST /omdsh-editor/open` | The launch: the session's own working directory, handed to a detached child process |
| The remembered choice | `localStorage` in the browser half, which is what lets the left half of the control be a verb |

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · What it adds：Nothing in the harness is modified. The three routes ride one prefix registration on `webServer`, the control sits in a published seat, and the package declares no slot of its own — so removing the row leaves the header exactly as it shipped.

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Which machine the editor opens on：**The one running the runtime.** That is where the project directory is, which makes it the only machine where opening the folder means anything, and it is where the harness's own model already puts the work.
section: Which machine the editor opens on

text: @omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Which machine the editor opens on：It follows that reaching a runtime over the network and pressing an editor starts that editor next to the files, not next to the browser. The plugin says so rather than hiding it: on a host with nothing installed the menu names the platform it looked on (`No editor found on the machine running dsh (linux)`), which distinguishes "install an editor" from "this runtime is not on your desk".
section: Which machine the editor opens on

text: @omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Which machine the editor opens on：Putting this in the Electron shell instead would have made the capability exclusive to the packaged application, when `dsh web` in a terminal wants it just as much.
section: Which machine the editor opens on

text:
@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · What it offers：| Kind | Applications |
|---|---|
| Editors | VS Code, VS Code Insiders, Cursor, Windsurf, Zed, Sublime Text, IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, Xcode |
| Files | Finder, File Explorer, File Manager (`xdg-open`) |
| Terminals | Terminal, iTerm2, Warp, Ghostty, WezTerm, kitty, Alacritty |

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · What it offers：Only the ones this host actually has are listed. Detection is a `stat` per candidate and nothing else — no `mdfind`, no registry read, no subprocess — so the whole sweep is a few milliseconds and the menu is a plain list rather than a dialog to wait on. The result is cached for 15 seconds, which is short enough that an editor installed while the harness runs shows up without a restart.

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · What it offers：An application this table does not know is invisible. Adding one is a dozen lines in [`src/catalog.ts`](src/catalog.ts), or an `editors` entry in the plugin's configuration, which replaces the shipped table outright — see [configuring it](#configuring-it).

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · How an application is found and started：A row lists the ways it may be present, most preferred first, and the first that answers decides both that it is installed and how it is launched.
section: How an application is found and started

text:
@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · How an application is found and started：| Probe | Where it looks | How it launches |
|---|---|---|
| `mac-app` | the standard macOS application directories, including `~/Applications` | `open -a <bundle> <dir>` |
| `windows-exe` | a fixed path under `%LOCALAPPDATA%` / `%ProgramFiles%` | the executable, with the directory |
| `path-bin` | `PATH` (with `.exe`/`.cmd`/`.bat`/`.com` on Windows) | the executable, with the directory |
section: How an application is found and started

text: @omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · How an application is found and started：The bundle is preferred over a CLI shim because it survives a GUI session whose `PATH` never ran the user's profile. `open -a` rather than the executable inside the bundle, because Launch Services is what activates an instance that is already running and the only way an argument reaches it — which is also what makes Terminal spawn a shell in the directory and Finder reveal it.
section: How an application is found and started

text: @omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · How an application is found and started：Four terminals (Ghostty, WezTerm, kitty, Alacritty) are listed by their CLI only. Their working directory is a flag rather than a document, and `open -a` cannot pass a flag to a running instance; a bundle probe would light the row up and then open the wrong directory, which is worse than the row being absent.
section: How an application is found and started

text: @omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · How an application is found and started：The child is detached into its own process group with its streams closed and then unreferenced, so quitting the harness — or one of the desktop shell's own memory-policy restarts — does not close the window you are typing in.
section: How an application is found and started

text: @omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Configuring it：**This plugin registers no settings namespace**, so its card in the plugin hub — titled **External Editor** there, from the `dsh.plughub` metadata in `package.json` — carries no form and honestly says it has nothing to configure. There is nothing a person tunes while using it: which applications exist is the host's answer, and which one the left half opens is remembered from the last press.

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Configuring it：What it does take is composition configuration, written on the bundle row in the profile's `cordis.patch.yml`:

```yaml
- id: editor
  name: '@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor'
  config:
    editors:                                  # replaces the shipped table outright

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Configuring it：`editors` is the whole table, not an addition to it: naming one row means that row is the only application offered, so a deployment adding one usually copies the shipped set from [`src/catalog.ts`](src/catalog.ts) first. `args` may be given for a launcher that spells its working directory as a flag (`['--working-directory={dir}']`); absent, the directory is simply appended, which is what every editor's CLI shim already means.

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Configuring it：`detectionTtlMs` is how long one detection sweep stays fresh. The default is short enough that an editor installed while the harness runs shows up without a restart, and there is rarely a reason to change it.

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · The routes：All three live under `/omdsh-editor` and are registered through `ctx.effect`, so unmounting the plugin removes them.

| Route | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /omdsh-editor/editors` | the applications this host has, and its `process.platform` |
| `GET /omdsh-editor/icon?id=…` | one application's own icon, as PNG |
| `POST /omdsh-editor/open` | launch one on a conversation's directory |

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · The routes：**The directory is the host's to decide.** An open request names a session; the session's own working directory is authoritative, and the `cwd` the browser sends is consulted only when the session carries none. Either way the result must be absolute and must still be a directory before anything is started. There is deliberately no `process.cwd()` fallback: opening whatever directory the harness happened to be started from, because this conversation has none, is a surprise rather than a fallback.

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · The routes：Every route passes the same browser-trust check the `/api` gateway applies ([`src/trust-fence.ts`](src/trust-fence.ts)) — a Host header naming us, plus same-origin browser markers. A route that starts a native application must be exactly as reachable as `/api`, and no more.

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · The control：One entry in `conversation.session.header.utilities`, the right-aligned utility row ui-conversation already declares. The package declares no slot of its own, so removing it leaves the header as it shipped.

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · The control：The split is the design. The left half is the verb — the common case is "open my project in my editor", and it should cost one press with no decision. The right half is the chooser, needed the first time and when you want a different one. The choice is remembered in `localStorage`, which is the only reason the left half can be a verb at all.
@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · The icons are the real ones：Each row is drawn with the product's actual icon, which is what makes six rows tell themselves apart the way a Dock does.
section: The icons are the real ones

text: @omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · The icons are the real ones：Nothing is bundled and nothing is redrawn. The bytes come off the copy of the application installed on this host — `Contents/Resources/*.icns`, named by the bundle's own `Info.plist` — rendered locally, exactly as the platform's "Open With" menu renders them. A package that shipped a dozen vendors' logos would be a licensing question; reading the copy the user installed is not.
section: The icons are the real ones

text: @omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · The icons are the real ones：Extraction is pure Node, no `sips` and no subprocess: an `.icns` is a flat type-length-value container, and every modern one carries its large variants as embedded PNG, so the icon is a scan and a slice. The smallest variant at least 64px wide is served, which is a few kilobytes and crisp at 2×.
section: The icons are the real ones

text: @omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · The icons are the real ones：Three things can leave a row without one — a host whose applications are not macOS bundles, a bundle using a compiled asset catalog rather than an `.icns`, and one whose `Resources` holds many `.icns` with none identifiable as the app's own. All three fall back to a glyph of the row's kind tinted in the product's accent, which is still enough to tell the rows apart. The catalog answer carries `icon: boolean` so the picker only requests icons that exist, and the `` falls back on error anyway.
section: The icons are the real ones

text:
@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Install：That is the [plugin hub](https://github.com/omdsh-plugins/omdsh-plughub)'s
installer with argv where the button was. It resolves this plugin from the
collection's [registry](https://github.com/omdsh-plugins/registry), installs it
from its GitHub repository, and writes the pnpm build-allowlist entry a bare
`dsh plugin add github:…` would leave to you — the entry carries the commit pnpm
resolved, so it can be copied out of a failure and never written down in
advance.

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Install：`dsh plugin --profile web add @omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor` is **not** that command yet:
this package is not on npm, and pnpm answers `ERR_PNPM_FETCH_404`. The same
install is also a button, on this plugin's card in **Settings → Plugins → Plugin
hub**, once the hub itself is in the profile.

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Install：`dsh plugin --profile <name> <args…>` is a thin `pnpm` forwarder run inside the profile directory (`~/.dsh/profiles/web`, or `$DSH_HOME/profiles/web`). It takes anything pnpm takes, and then reconciles `dsh.profile.bundles` against what is installed.

Or from a checkout, which is what working on the plugin itself wants:

```sh
pnpm install && pnpm run build                 # lib/ must exist; a path install never runs prepare
dsh plugin --profile web add "$PWD"
```

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Install：A relative spec is anchored to the directory you invoked `dsh` from. Either way the profile manifest gains the dependency and `@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor` is appended to `dsh.profile.bundles`, so [`cordis.patch.yml`](cordis.patch.yml) is applied after `@deepseek-ai/dsh-base` and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-web-app`. The harness tree stays exactly as it shipped.

Restart the runtime to pick it up (`dsh web`, or quit and reopen the desktop application). Remove it the same way:

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Install：```sh
dsh plugin --profile web remove @omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor
```

which takes the bundle row, the routes, and the control with it, leaving the session header as it shipped.

A checkout install records a `link:`, which means pnpm neither builds the package nor installs its dependencies — neither matters here, because the node half imports only Node builtins and the browser half inlines `clsx`. It does mean a rebuild after editing sources is yours to run.

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Install：**There is no companion plugin to be absent.** Every service either half injects is a harness one the profile already composes — `webServer`, `sessions`, and `webRuntime` on the host, `slots` and `locale` in the browser — so nothing else from this collection has to be installed beside it, and nothing else changes what it does. `webRuntime` is the web surface bundle's, which is what makes this a web-profile row: it carries the trust list the fence checks against, and a surface with no web server has no browser to serve anyway.

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Commands：```sh
pnpm install
pnpm run build       # tsc emits lib/types, tsdown bundles both halves
pnpm run typecheck   # sources and tests
pnpm run test        # vitest

The committed manifest pins the published harness, so a bare clone installs and builds itself. To build against a sibling checkout instead:

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Commands：```sh
pnpm run harness:local ../../deepseek-harness   # that checkout must be built first
pnpm install
pnpm run harness:npm                            # before committing — a link: is one machine's layout
pnpm run check:harness-pin

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Commands：The node-only specs run from a bare clone on the pin. The three browser specs need the checkout: the harness's published browser packages ship a loader bundle a test runner cannot import, so on the pin they resolve to [`tests/registry-mode-guard.ts`](tests/registry-mode-guard.ts) and fail with a message saying so.

@omdsh-plugins/omdsh-editor README · Known limitations：- **Editors are found from a table.** A host with something unusual installed sees a shorter list than it has. "What editors exist on this machine" is not a question with an answer; the escape hatch is the `editors` configuration.
- **Success means the process started.** Once the child is detached there is no exit code to wait for, so an editor that starts and then refuses the directory itself reports nothing back. The spawn window is 150ms — long enough for Node to deliver an `ENOENT`, short enough to be invisible.
- **The remembered choice is per browser, not per user.** It lives in `localStorage`, so a second browser starts on the first listed editor again.
- **Xcode is handed a directory, not a project.** `open -a Xcode <dir>` is what the row does; a folder that is not a project or workspace opens as Xcode's own folder view.
- **Windows detection covers the default install locations only.** An editor installed elsewhere is found only if its shim is on `PATH`.
- **Icons are macOS-only.** Windows would need PE resource extraction and Linux a `.desktop` + theme lookup; neither is done, so those hosts get the kind glyph. A bund
